content: Steroid diabetes is a condition characterized by prolonged high blood sugar levels (hyperglycemia) that result from the use of glucocorticoid medications prescribed for other medical conditions. This condition is often temporary but not always. The glucocorticoids most commonly associated with steroid diabetes are prednisone and dexamethasone, which are administered systemically in pharmacologic doses over a period of days or weeks. Steroid diabetes frequently develops during high-dose glucocorticoid therapy for conditions such as severe asthma, organ transplantation, cystic fibrosis, inflammatory bowel disease, or during induction chemotherapy for leukemia or other cancers. Glucocorticoids interfere with the action of insulin and promote gluconeogenesis, particularly in the liver, leading to an overall increase in glucose production by the liver. While most individuals can produce sufficient additional insulin to counteract this effect and maintain normal blood sugar levels, those who cannot compensate develop steroid diabetes. The diagnostic criteria for steroid diabetes are the same as those for other forms of diabetes. These include fasting blood glucose levels consistently above 125 mg/dL (7 mmol/L) or random blood glucose levels exceeding 200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L) in the context of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy. Insulin levels in affected individuals are typically detectable and may even be elevated, but they are insufficient to adequately control blood sugar levels. In severe cases, the hyperglycemia can become extreme enough to result in a nonketotic hyperosmolar coma. The treatment approach for steroid diabetes depends on the severity of the hyperglycemia and the anticipated duration of glucocorticoid therapy. Mild hyperglycemia in an otherwise healthy individual may not require treatment if the glucocorticoids are expected to be discontinued within one to two weeks. However, moderate hyperglycemia increases the risk of infections, particularly fungal infections, especially in individuals with additional risk factors such as immunosuppression or the presence of central intravenous lines. Insulin is the most commonly used treatment for managing steroid diabetes. It is important to differentiate steroid diabetes from other causes of hyperglycemia, such as stress-induced hyperglycemia, hyperglycemia caused by excessive intravenous glucose administration, or newly diagnosed diabetes of another type. In some cases, glucocorticoid therapy may unmask preexisting but undiagnosed type 2 diabetes, as subclinical hyperglycemia worsens and becomes symptomatic. Additionally, glucocorticoid treatment can sometimes precipitate the onset of type 1 or type 2 diabetes in individuals who are already predisposed to developing these conditions. As a result, it is not always possible to determine whether steroid diabetes will resolve after glucocorticoid therapy is discontinued or whether it will persist as a permanent form of diabetes. In general, steroid diabetes that occurs in individuals without preexisting type 2 diabetes tends to resolve once glucocorticoid therapy is stopped. It is also worth noting that steroid diabetes does not occur with other types of steroid hormones, such as anabolic steroids, mineralocorticoids, or sex steroids, as these categories of steroids have minimal impact on glucose metabolism.
